summary: This unit teaches you to plan, research, write, present and file formal technical reports in a fabrication workshop: investigation and incident reports, inspection and test reports, non-conformance reports, progress reports and feasibility reports. You will learn to agree terms of reference, gather sound evidence, find root causes, keep findings, conclusions and recommendations apart, present figures honestly in tables and charts, write clearly and objectively, and handle review, approval, confidentiality, records and follow-up.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). 'Advanced' means formal reports of several sections, written for managers, clients, inspectors or a board, and based on evidence you gather and analyse yourself: why welds keep failing, what happened in an accident, whether a batch meets the specification, how a contract is going, or which of two machines the Centre should buy.

Decisions, money and safety rest on these reports. A clear, honest report gets a problem fixed for good. A vague one wastes the reader's time; one that leaves out a failed test can put lives at risk and the business in court.
**Who it is for:** Welding Level 3 trainees at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres, and welders, inspectors and team leaders who report to managers and clients.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in practice
rows: Agree its purpose, scope, readers, deadline and approver (the terms of reference), and set a timetable.
Collect primary and secondary evidence, measure and photograph properly, interview fairly, and keep the evidence and people's personal details safe.
Work out the figures, find the root cause with a recognised method, and draw conclusions that follow from the evidence.
Choose tables, charts and pictures that make each point clearly and honestly.
Use the right sections in the right order for the type of report, with an executive summary and appendices.
Use plain, objective, consistent language that the readers will understand.
Control versions, answer review comments, get approval, and send the report only to the right people.
Present the findings, close out non-conformances, and check that recommendations were carried out and worked.

ul: A **multiple-choice paper** on types of report, planning, evidence, analysis, charts, structure, style, review, confidentiality and records, with some percentage and average sums.

A **written paper**: short answers needing exact terms (terms of reference, caption, objective, active voice, title page, root cause analysis, audience, median, mode, range) and sums; and longer answers in full sentences, such as planning an investigation or writing an executive summary.

**Practical tasks** done as a group: investigate a staged weld quality problem and write a formal investigation report; and prepare and present a feasibility report comparing two options, with a cost table in J$ and GCT shown at the current rate.

blocks.note: In the practicals, each member writes and signs at least one section, checks another member's section, and answers the comments on their own. Keep a version record from the first draft.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Reports, readers and terms of reference

head: Type of report
What it is for
Example
rows: Find what happened and why, and stop it happening again
A trainee hurt when a cylinder fell
Record checks or tests and whether the item meets the requirement
Bend tests on six welder test coupons
Record work or material that does not meet a requirement, and the action taken
Handrails made to an old drawing revision
Compare work done with the plan, with reasons and next steps
Buy or keep hiring a site welding machine
Record work done on equipment and its condition
Six-monthly check of the Centre's welding sets
Record what was done and hand over the records
A staircase handed over with its inspection records

blocks.p: The **audience** is the people a report is written for. Their needs set its length, words and level of detail. Ask: What do they already know? What will they decide or do? How much time will they give it? Will they read it on paper or a phone? Is English their first language?

ul: A board or a manager wants the answer, the cost and the decision needed, quickly: give it in the executive summary.
An inspector or engineer wants the evidence and the method: give it in the body and the appendices.
The workshop team wants to know what changes for them: give it plainly, and present it to them in person.

blocks.p: The **terms of reference** are the agreed statement of what the report will do, set with the person who asks for it, before any work starts:

ul: **Purpose:** the question the report must answer.
**Scope:** which jobs, dates, places and people it covers, and what it does not.
**Readers:** who will receive it.
**Deadline and approver:** when it is due and who signs it off.
Any limits: length, format, budget for tests.

blocks.note: Example: 'To find why MIG fillet welds on the trailer frames made in Bay 2 between 1 and 31 October failed inspection, and to recommend actions. Report to the Workshop Manager by 24 November 2026; approved by the QC Supervisor.' Every later choice about evidence and length goes back to this.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Work back from the deadline, counting working days, and leave time for review. Example: a report due 12 working days from Monday 9 November 2026 (day 1) is due on Tuesday 24 November.

head: Working days
Stage
rows: Gather evidence: records, measurements, tests, photos, interviews
Review by the supervisor; answer comments

blocks.p: Plan the headings early too: then you know what evidence each section needs before you start collecting it.

head: Primary evidence (first-hand)
Secondary evidence (from others)
rows: Logs and records: oven log, machine settings sheets, inspection sheets
Statements from people involved and witnesses
Treat advertisements and online forums with caution: they are not independent or checked

blocks.p: The report must say how its facts were gathered, so readers can judge how far to rely on them: what was measured or tested, with what instrument, by whom, when, and how many.

ul: If you check a **sample**, say so: '30 of the 300 brackets were checked'.
Say how the sample was chosen: at random, every tenth item, or all items from one bay or one day. Never choose the best-looking ones, and never imply that everything was checked.
State the limits honestly: 'The frames already sent to the client could not be checked.'
Speak to each person separately, soon after the event, somewhere quiet.
Explain that the aim is to find causes, not to blame.
Ask open, neutral questions: 'Tell me what you saw, step by step.' 'What happened next?'
Avoid leading or blaming questions such as 'You didn't check the chain, did you?': they shape the answer and shut people down.
Write down their own words, read the statement back, and ask them to sign and date it.
Do not repair, clean, move or throw away damaged items until they have been recorded, unless that is needed to make the area safe. Tag them and store them.
Keep the **original** records (inspection sheets, logs, statements) even after their data has been typed into the report: they are the proof, and they may be needed to check a figure.
Use calibrated instruments, write the unit with every measurement, and repeat important ones.
Mark any figure that is an **estimate** as an estimate, and say how it was worked out, so readers know how far to rely on it.
Take them at the time, in good light, with a ruler or tape in the shot for size.
Take a wide shot to show where, then the close-up.
Never edit a photo in a way that changes what it shows; keep the original files.
Number each photo and give it a **caption**: what it shows, where and when, and who took it.

blocks.note: Personal details, such as an injured person's medical information, are confidential. They go only to people who need them, and are kept out of copies sent outside the organisation. Jamaica's data protection law requires organisations to protect personal information.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Analysis: root causes, findings and conclusions

head: Part
What it is
Example (trailer frame welds)
rows: A fact found, measured or seen, with no opinion added
'9 of the 25 sectioned welds showed lack of fusion at the root. All 9 were made on machine M4, fitted on 6 October.'
What the findings mean, worked out from the evidence
'The most likely cause was the low voltage set on M4, which was set from the old machine's settings sheet and did not meet the WPS.'
What should be done, by whom and by when, and how it will be checked
'From 23 November the QC Supervisor will check every machine's settings against the WPS each Monday and sign the settings sheet. The reject rate will be reviewed on 18 December.'

blocks.p: Keeping the three apart lets the reader see the evidence before the opinion, and judge whether the conclusion really follows.

The **root cause** is the basic reason something happened, which, if fixed, stops it happening again. The fault you see (lack of fusion) is a symptom; 'the welder was careless' is rarely the root cause, because it does not explain why the system allowed it. **Root cause analysis (RCA)** uses a method such as the five whys or a fishbone diagram.

flow: Why did the frames fail inspection? Lack of fusion at the root of the fillet welds.
Why was there lack of fusion? The voltage was too low for the wire feed speed.
Why was the voltage too low? M4 was set from the settings sheet for the old machine.
Why was the old sheet used? Nobody checked the settings when M4 replaced the old machine.
Why was there no check? The shop has no procedure for checking settings when equipment is replaced. This is the root cause.

blocks.p: The problem is written at the head of the 'fish', and possible causes are grouped along the bones under headings. A common set for a workshop problem:

head: Heading
Possible causes of lack of fusion
rows: WPS not followed; no settings check after a machine change
Wrong voltage; worn contact tip; wire feed slipping
Mill scale or rust on the plate; wrong wire
Welder not trained on the new machine; torch angle
Inspection missed it; no sectioning on first-off frames

blocks.p: A **Pareto chart** ranks causes from the most common to the least, with a running total. It usually shows that a few causes make most of the problems, so they are tackled first.
Here three defect types make 80% of the problems. ('Other' goes last, whatever its size.)

When something 'does not meet the specification', say exactly which requirement, the value measured, and the verdict: 'Leg length required: 6 mm minimum (drawing T-12, revision C). Measured: 4.5 mm. Does not meet the requirement.'

head: Weak
Strong
rows: 'The QC Supervisor will check every machine's settings against the WPS each Monday from 23 November and sign the settings sheet.'
'The Workshop Manager will arrange a two-hour session on M4's settings for all Bay 2 welders by 4 December.'

head: Figure
Method
Example
rows: Re-work fell from 64 to 48 hours a month: 16 ÷ 64 × 100 = 25% less
the middle value, once the values are in order (with an even number, the average of the middle two)
the value that appears most often

blocks.note: A fall from 10% to 8% is a fall of 2 **percentage points**, but a fall of 20% in the rate (2 ÷ 10 × 100). Say which you mean.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: **Time:** convert to decimal hours before multiplying: 2 h 15 min = 2.25 h; 50 min = 50 ÷ 60 = 0.83 h.
**Money:** in J$, with GCT on its own line 'at the current rate'; check that the totals add up.
**Rounding:** use the same number of decimal places through a table; do not give false precision such as 12.3456%.

**Spreadsheets:** formulas cut copying mistakes and update when a figure changes. Check them: show the formulas, test one line by hand, check totals, label units, and keep a copy of the file used for the report.

head: To show
Use
Example
rows: Exact figures that readers must look up
Leg sizes measured on 20 fillet welds
Rejected welds for each of four bays
The monthly reject rate over a year
Shares of one whole, with few parts
Which few causes give most problems
Defect types ranked, with a running total
How measurements spread around a size
How many of 200 fillet welds fall in each 0.5 mm band

blocks.h: Rules for every table and chart

ul: A **number and a title**: 'Figure 3: Monthly reject rate, Bay 2, January to October 2026'. The text can then point to it.
Axes labelled, with units; a key (legend) where there is more than one series; the source of the data.
Start the value axis at zero unless there is a clear reason not to, and say so if you do not. A graph that starts at 90 can make a small change look huge.
One main message per chart, and a sentence in the text that says what it shows.
Long raw data, such as 200 measurements, goes in an **appendix**, with a short summary table in the body.
Photos: numbered, captioned, with a scale, referred to in the text.
Sketches: neat and labelled; marked 'not to scale' if they are not. A marked-up sketch is often the clearest way to show where each faulty weld was.
Drawings from the job: copied with their number and **revision**, marked up clearly (for example, weld numbers circled).
Put in the body only the pictures that support a finding; others go in an appendix.

head: Section
What it contains
rows: Title, report number, author, date, version, and who it is for
Each version, its date, what changed and who changed it
The purpose, key findings, conclusions, recommendations and costs, on one page or less
Background, terms of reference and scope
How the evidence was gathered and analysed
The facts, with tables, charts and photos
What the findings mean; the root cause
The answers to the purpose, drawn from the evidence
Actions, each with an owner and a date
The documents, standards and sources used, with editions and revisions
Raw data, full statements, extra photos, calculations
Terms and short forms some readers may not know, where needed

blocks.p: Number sections and sub-sections (1, 1.1, 1.2) so readers and reviewers can refer to them. Name the edition of each standard and the revision of each drawing used: requirements change between editions, and the reader must know exactly which ones applied.

ul: **Test report:** test piece identity, material and WPS, test method, acceptance criteria, results, pass or fail, who tested, date, and signatures.
**Progress report:** work done against the plan, delays and their reasons, the forecast finish, problems and next steps.
**Feasibility report:** background, the options, the criteria used to compare them, a cost table, a scoring table, risks, conclusions and a recommendation.
**NCR:** usually a form; see the section on review, approval and records.

blocks.p: Write it **last**, when the findings and recommendations are settled. It must stand on its own, so that a busy reader can decide without reading further. Example:

blocks.note: This report compares buying an engine-driven welding machine with continuing to hire one for site jobs. In the last 12 months the shop hired a machine on 46 days at J$9 500 a day, a total of J$437 000. A new machine of the same size would cost about J$1 150 000 plus GCT at the current rate, with fuel, servicing and insurance of about J$120 000 a year. At the present level of site work, buying would save about J$317 000 a year and pay for itself in under four years, and the machine would be on hand for urgent jobs. We recommend buying one machine, with a service contract, in the next financial year.
blocks.label: Example

blocks.p: It works because it gives the purpose, the evidence in brief with figures, the cost (with GCT shown as 'at the current rate'), and a clear recommendation, in plain words.

ul: **Objective:** state facts, with times, numbers and identities; no blame, emotion or guesses dressed as facts. Where an opinion is needed, label it as one.
**Active voice:** 'The inspector rejected six welds' is clearer than 'Six welds were rejected by the inspector'. Use the passive only when who did it is unknown or does not matter.
**Plain words and short sentences:** 'use', not 'utilise'; 'start', not 'commence'; one idea per sentence, usually under about 20 words.
**The same word for the same thing:** if you write 'work clamp', do not switch to 'earth clamp' and 'ground clamp': readers will think they are different things.
**Explain terms and short forms** the first time: 'welding procedure specification (WPS)'. Add a glossary if there are many.
**Units with every number,** metric first: 6 mm, 120 A, 15 L/min.
**Dates that cannot be misread:** '5 November 2026', not '5/11/26', which a reader used to American dates takes as 11 May.
**British spelling,** as used in Jamaica, with the spell-checker set to UK English; then proofread anyway.

head: Unclear or biased
Clear and objective
rows: 'The careless night shift did the welds badly again.'
'Six of the 14 welds made on the night shift of 4 November had undercut deeper than 0.5 mm.'
'18 of 150 welds (12%) failed visual inspection between 2 and 13 November.'
'At this moment in time, utilisation of grinder G2 without its guard was observed.'
'At 10:20 a.m. on 6 November, grinder G2 was in use without its guard.'
'Please check the WPS by Friday 13 November.'

head: Short form
Meaning
Example
rows: 'the low-hydrogen electrodes, i.e. the E7018 in the oven'
Avoid in formal reports: list the items
Use in tables where a column does not apply

blocks.h: Readers on phones, or reading in a second language

ul: Put the key points and recommendations at the top.
Use headings, numbered sections, short paragraphs, lists and narrow tables.
Use photos and simple sketches with captions where words are hard.
Send a file type that opens on any phone, such as PDF.
Ask someone from the readership to read the draft before it is issued.
Number and date every draft: v0.1, v0.2 and so on. The first issued copy is v1.0; a later corrected issue is v1.1 or v2.0.
Keep a change record at the front: version, date, what changed, who changed it.
Name files clearly, with the version and date: 'INV-031_Trailer-Frames_v0.2_2026-11-12'.
Mark old versions as superseded, so nobody works from them.

flow: A competent person (supervisor, inspector) reviews the draft for accuracy, missing facts, figures and wording
The writer answers every comment: changes the report, or explains why not
The comments and answers are recorded
The person with authority approves and signs
Only the approved version is issued, to the people on the distribution list

blocks.p: On a contract, clients, inspectors and the team make decisions and payments from reports. If people work from different versions, mistakes, disputes and extra cost follow; a clear record shows who said what, and when.

ul: Share personal details (medical information, home addresses) and a client's prices and drawings only with people who need them.
When an outside body needs part of a report, send only the parts it needs, without personal details, and only with approval.
Store reports securely: a locked cabinet, a password-protected folder.

blocks.p: A report must be accurate and complete. Never leave out a finding, soften it or change a figure because it is awkward for someone. If you are pressed to, explain that the report must be accurate, and raise it with a higher manager if the pressure continues. Record what happened.

flow: Find the non-conformance; tag the items and keep them apart
Raise the NCR: number, date, job, drawing and revision, the requirement, what was found (with measurements and photos), quantity, who found it
Decide the disposition, and have it approved
Find the cause; plan corrective action with an owner and a date
Re-inspect the items after rework or repair
Check that the corrective action has worked
Close, sign and file the NCR

head: Disposition
Meaning
rows: Make the item meet the requirement, for example re-cut and re-weld to the right drawing
Make it fit for use by an approved repair method, even if not exactly to the original requirement
Accept it as it stands; only with the client's or designer's written agreement

blocks.note: Putting the faulty items right is the **correction**. Stopping the same thing happening again is the **corrective action**, and it must tackle the root cause. An NCR is closed only when the items are acceptable **and** the corrective action has been checked and found to work.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: File the approved report with its original evidence for as long as the Centre's rules or the contract require, in a way that lets it be found again.

Present the findings: to the workshop team at a toolbox talk, give the key points simply, show one or two charts, say what changes for them and take questions; to a manager, give the summary and the decision needed.
Follow up each recommendation on its due date: was it done, and did it work (for example, has the reject rate fallen)? Record the result.

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say 'I can' to a line, go back to that section and practise it with your instructor.

ul: I can name the main types of technical report and say what each is for.
I can agree terms of reference and plan a timetable back from the deadline.
I can write for different readers, including busy managers and people reading on phones or in a second language.
I can gather primary and secondary evidence, describe my method and sample, and keep evidence safe.
I can interview people fairly with open, neutral questions.
I can take and caption photographs that work as evidence.
I can find a root cause with the five whys or a fishbone diagram, and rank causes with a Pareto chart.
I can keep findings, conclusions and recommendations apart, and write recommendations with an owner and a date.
I can work out rates, percentage changes, means, medians, modes and ranges, and tell percentage points from percentages.
I can choose the right table or chart and present data honestly.
I can set out a formal report in the right order, with an executive summary written last.
I can write objectively and clearly, in the active voice, with consistent terms, units and unambiguous dates.
I can control versions, answer review comments, and issue only approved reports to the right people.
I can protect confidential details and stay honest under pressure.
I can take an NCR from discovery to close-out, and follow up recommendations.

terms: Active voice
A sentence in which the doer comes first: 'The inspector rejected the weld'
Appendix
A section at the end for raw data, full statements and extra material
Audience
The people a report is written for
Caption
The short text under a photo or figure saying what it shows
Conclusion
What the findings mean, drawn from the evidence
Corrective action
Action that removes the cause of a problem so it does not happen again
Disposition
The decision on what to do with non-conforming work: rework, repair, use as is, or scrap
Distribution list
The list of people who receive a copy of a report
Executive summary
A short summary at the front giving the key findings, conclusions and recommendations
Finding
A fact found, measured or seen
Fishbone diagram
A cause-and-effect diagram grouping possible causes under headings
Five whys
Asking 'why?' again and again until the root cause is reached
Non-conformance report (NCR)
A record of work or material that does not meet a requirement, and the action taken
Objective
Based on facts, free of personal feelings and blame
Pareto chart
A chart ranking causes from most to least common, with a running total
Primary evidence
Evidence gathered first-hand: measurements, records, photos, statements
Recommendation
An action the report says should be taken, with an owner and a date
Root cause
The basic reason a problem happened, which, if fixed, stops it happening again
Root cause analysis (RCA)
Using a method to find the root cause of a problem
Secondary evidence
Information from other sources: standards, makers' data, books
Terms of reference
The agreed purpose, scope, readers, deadline and limits of a report
Title page
The first page, with the title, report number, author, date and version
Version control
Numbering and dating each draft so that everyone knows which is current

c1.title: Trailer frame welds in Lionel Town
c1.text: Marsha Blake, the QC officer at a fabrication shop in Lionel Town, Clarendon, is asked by the manager, Mr Clarke, to report on why MIG fillet welds on boat-trailer frames have been failing inspection since early October. She sections 25 welds from frames made in Bay 2 and finds lack of fusion in 9 of them. All 9 were made on a replacement welding machine fitted on 6 October, and its voltage had been set from the settings sheet written for the old machine.

c2.title: A fallen cylinder at a training centre in Brown's Town
c2.text: During an evening class at a training centre in Brown's Town, St Ann, an argon cylinder slid off a cylinder trolley and broke a trainee's toe. The instructor, Damion Ricketts, must write the incident report for the Centre manager. He finds that the trolley's restraining chain had been broken for about three weeks, that a trainee had mentioned it to a technician, and that the weekly equipment check sheet has no entries for those weeks. The trainee's medical notes are in the file.

c3.title: A year's quality figures in Mandeville
c3.text: Abigail Ferguson, QC officer at a fabrication shop in Mandeville, Manchester, is preparing the shop's quality report. The monthly weld reject rate fell from 9.0% in January to 5.4% in October. In October the defects found were: porosity 26, undercut 18, lack of fusion 8, slag inclusions 5, cracks 2, other 6. She also has the leg lengths of 200 fillet welds measured in October, against a drawing size of 6 mm.

c4.title: New welding sets for a contractor in Ocho Rios
c4.text: A building contractor in Ocho Rios, St Ann, asks its site supervisor, Leon Shaw, to report on whether to replace its four old transformer welding sets with four inverter sets. The new sets would cost J$720 000 in total, plus GCT at the current rate; they would cut electricity costs by about J$15 000 a month; and the old sets can be sold for J$80 000 in total. The report goes to the company's directors and to the welders who will use the machines.

c5.title: An NCR on hotel handrails in St Ann's Bay
c5.text: At a steel fabricator in St Ann's Bay, St Ann, the QC officer, Kerene Walters, has raised a non-conformance report. Fourteen handrail sections for a hotel were made to drawing H-07 revision B, although revision C, issued two weeks earlier, raised the rail height by 50 mm. Old copies of revision B were still pinned up in the fabrication bay. Her draft report is version 0.2, and the hotel's project engineer will receive the issued copy.

questions.q: What percentage of the welds Marsha sectioned showed lack of fusion?
questions.why: 9 ÷ 25 × 100 = 36%. The report should also say that the 25 were a sample from Bay 2, and how they were chosen, so readers know how far the figure applies.

questions.q: Marsha follows the chain of causes back. Which one should her analysis name as the basic reason the frames failed?
o: Lack of fusion was found in the fillet welds on the frames
No check of the settings is made when a machine is replaced
The two welders did not look at their own welds carefully enough
The replacement machine fitted on 6 October was faulty
questions.why: Lack of fusion is the symptom, and the machine itself was not faulty: it was set wrongly. Blaming the welders does not explain why the system let the wrong settings through. Without a settings check after a machine change, it will happen again.

questions.q: Marsha's draft says: 'The new machine makes bad welds.' Which rewrite is best?
o: 9 of 25 sectioned welds made on M4 after 6 October lacked fusion.
The new machine is clearly not as good as the one it replaced.
Most of the welds made on the new machine seem to be quite poor.
Welders and inspectors agree that the new machine makes bad welds.
questions.why: An objective finding gives the facts, numbers and identities, with no judgement. 'Bad', 'seem' and 'clearly' are opinions, and the original sentence blames the machine when the fault was in how it was set.

questions.q: Marsha wants to show where on the frames the 9 faulty welds were. Which is best?
o: A paragraph describing the position of each weld in words
A sketch of a frame with each weld numbered, marked 'not to scale'
A photo of the whole bay, taken from the door, with the frames in it
A list of the 9 weld numbers in the appendix, with no other detail
questions.why: A labelled sketch shows positions far more clearly than words, and marking it 'not to scale' stops anyone measuring from it. Close-up photos with a ruler can then show each fault.

questions.q: What should Damion do with the trolley before the investigation is finished?
o: Repair the chain straight away so the trolley is safe for the next class
Take it out of use, tag it, and keep it unrepaired as evidence
Throw it out and buy a new trolley before the Centre manager asks
Leave it in the bay with a sign telling trainees not to use it
questions.why: The broken chain is key evidence and must be recorded and kept as found, while the trolley is made unusable so nobody else is hurt. Repairing or discarding it first destroys the evidence.

questions.q: Using the five whys, which question takes Damion closest to the root cause?
o: Why was the injured trainee standing so close to the trolley?
Why did the cylinder slide off to the left side, not the right?
Why was a broken chain not recorded or repaired for three weeks?
Why was the class using argon rather than another shielding gas?
questions.why: The chain was broken for weeks, it was mentioned, and the check sheet was blank: something in the checking and reporting system failed. Asking why leads to that system cause, which is what must be fixed.

questions.q: How should the trainee's medical notes be handled in the report?
o: Include them in an appendix, so that the report gives the full facts
Put them in the findings, as the main evidence of the injury
Pin them up with the safety notice, so all trainees see the result
Describe the injury briefly; keep the notes on the confidential file
questions.why: The report needs only a brief, factual description of the injury. Medical details are personal information, protected by the data protection law, and stay on a confidential file seen only by those who need it.

questions.q: What share of October's defects were porosity and undercut together?
o: About 40%
About 68%
About 80%
questions.why: The total is 26 + 18 + 8 + 5 + 2 + 6 = 65. Porosity and undercut are 44 of them: 44 ÷ 65 × 100 = about 68%. 44 is the number of defects, not the share; 80% is reached only when lack of fusion is added.

questions.q: By what percentage did the monthly reject rate fall from January to October?
questions.why: The fall is 9.0 − 5.4 = 3.6 percentage points, and 3.6 ÷ 9.0 × 100 = 40% of the January rate. A report should make clear which of the two it means.

questions.q: Which chart best shows how the 200 leg lengths are spread around the 6 mm drawing size?
o: A pie chart with one slice for every weld that was measured
A histogram showing how many welds fall in each size band
A Gantt chart showing the day on which each weld was made
A line graph joining the welds in alphabetical order of welder
questions.why: A histogram groups the measurements into bands (for example 5.5–6.0 mm) and shows how many fall in each, so the spread and any undersize welds are clear at a glance. The full 200 readings go in an appendix.

questions.q: About how long would the new sets take to pay for themselves from the electricity saving, before GCT?
o: About 53 months
48 months
About 5 months
About 43 months
questions.why: The net cost is J$720 000 − J$80 000 = J$640 000, and 640 000 ÷ 15 000 = about 43 months. Ignoring the sale of the old sets gives 48 months; adding the sale money instead of taking it away gives about 53.

questions.q: When should Leon write the executive summary?
o: First, so that it guides the evidence he goes on to collect
Last, once the findings and recommendation are settled
Halfway, after the costs but before the recommendation
Never: the directors can read the conclusions instead
questions.why: An executive summary sums up the whole report, including the recommendation, so it can only be written when those are final. The terms of reference, not the summary, guide what evidence to collect.

questions.q: Leon scores both options on safety, running cost, noise and portability. What makes the comparison fair?
o: Scoring each option on the same criteria, from the same kind of sources
Scoring the new sets on their strengths and the old ones on their faults
Leaving out any criterion on which the option he prefers scores lower
Asking only the supplier of the new sets for the figures to be scored
questions.why: A fair comparison uses the same measures for every option, with figures from comparable, independent sources, and keeps every criterion in, even where the preferred option loses. Otherwise the recommendation cannot be trusted.

questions.q: How should the price of the new sets be shown in Leon's cost table?
o: J$720 000 before tax, with GCT on its own line at the current rate
One figure with the GCT already added in, so it is simple to read
J$720 000 with GCT worked out at last year's rate, to keep it fixed
J$720 000 only, since the directors know that GCT is added on top
questions.why: Showing the price before tax and GCT on its own line, at the current rate, lets the directors see both figures. The rate can change, so an old rate must never be built into the figures.

questions.q: Which disposition for the 14 handrail sections may be used only with the hotel's written agreement?
o: Rework them to revision C
Scrap them and make new ones
Use them as they are
Hold them while the NCR is open
questions.why: Using non-conforming work as it stands is a concession: the client or designer must agree to it in writing. Rework to the current revision and scrapping both bring the work back to the requirement.

questions.q: Which corrective action deals with the cause of this non-conformance?
o: Re-make the 14 sections to the right height on drawing H-07 revision C
Remind the welders in the bay to read their drawings much more carefully in future
Ask the hotel's engineer whether the lower rails could be accepted after all
Withdraw and stamp old revisions whenever a new one is issued, using a register
questions.why: Re-making the sections is the correction for this batch. The cause was out-of-date copies left in the bay, so the corrective action is a controlled way of withdrawing old revisions, checked through a drawing register.

questions.q: Once the supervisor approves the report, what version should the copy sent to the hotel carry?
o: Version 0.3, the next number after the draft
Version 0.2, the last one that Kerene edited herself
No version number, since the report is final
Version 1.0, with the drafts marked superseded
questions.why: Drafts carry 0.x numbers; the first approved, issued copy is 1.0. The change record and the file name show it, and the drafts are marked as superseded so nobody works from them.

questions.q: When can Kerene close the NCR?
o: When the items pass inspection and the corrective action is shown to work
When the 14 sections have been re-made and sent to the hotel
When the hotel's engineer has received the final issued report
When the production manager has signed to say that the whole matter is now settled
questions.why: An NCR is closed only when the items are acceptable and the corrective action has been checked and found to work, for example by a check that no old revisions remain in the bay. Then it is signed off and filed.

questions.q: Six hardness readings from a weld are 182, 175, 190, 178, 186 and 175. What is their median?
questions.why: In order: 175, 175, 178, 182, 186, 190. With an even number of values, the median is the average of the middle two: (178 + 182) ÷ 2 = 180. 181 is the mean and 175 the mode.

questions.q: A report will be read by a client in the USA. Which way of writing the inspection date is clearest?
o: Thursday 05/11/26
5 November 2026
questions.why: Writing the month as a word cannot be misread. In the USA, 05/11/2026 is read as 11 May, so a date written only in figures may be taken as a different day; adding the weekday does not remove the doubt.
